thread.title: United to host discussion of exorcisms ahead of screening of 'The Exorcist' as part of 'Movies with Meaning' series
thread.title_full: United to host discussion of exorcisms ahead of screening of 'The Exorcist' as part of 'Movies with Meaning' series

author: Nancy Burns-Fusaro Sun staff writer
title: United to host discussion of exorcisms ahead of screening of 'The Exorcist' as part of 'Movies with Meaning' series
text:
WESTERLY — Have you ever wondered if exorcisms are real? Or if any actually ever take place — not just in the movies or science fiction, but in real life?
If so, then bring your wonderment and questions to the United Thursday night, and ask an exorcism expert everything you've ever wanted to know about "the prayer used against the power of the devil."
As part of the "Movies with Meaning" series, Peter Laffin, a local journalist has invited The Rev. Thomas F. X. Hoar from Enders Island to join him for a discussion prior to the screening of William Friedkin’s "The Exorcist" Thursday.
Fr. Hoar, a Roman Catholic priest with the Society of St. Edmund who is experienced in the ministry of healing and deliverance, will also join Laffin, a staff writer for the National Catholic Register, for a Q&A following the screening of the film.
One of the most profitable and classic horror movies ever made, "The Exorcist," is the tale of an exorcism based loosely on actual events.
When young Regan (played by Linda Blair) starts acting odd — levitating, speaking in tongues — her worried mother (Ellen Burstyn) seeks medical help, only to hit a dead end. A local priest (Jason Miller), however, thinks the girl may be seized by the devil. The priest makes a request to perform an exorcism, and the church sends in an expert (Max von Sydow) to help with the difficult job.
While based on a true story about a 12-year-old boy in need of exorcism, the movie packed all the elements of possession into one character.
"Possession is still very rare," said Hoar, the president and CEO of Ender’s Island, who plans to discuss the reality of the demonic, what happens at real-life exorcisms, and what can be done to prevent and combat "manifestations of evil" Thursday. But the need for exorcisms is on the rise.
"We are seeing a revival," Hoar said. "When I was ordained forty-eight years ago there was maybe one exorcist in this country."
"Today," he said, "there are almost four hundred and we can't keep up."
"We are in a great spiritual battle for the survival of God's people," Hoar said, "and most people are not even aware of it."
"The devil is real," he stressed, "and demons seek to separate people from their relationship with God."
"Demons cannot enter without being invited," Hoar said, explaining that often "they come through trauma."
Exorcism, said Hoar, is a specific form of prayer that the Roman Catholic Church uses against the power of the devil.
"The solemn rite of exorcism can only be performed with the authority of a bishop," said Hoar who explained that an exorcism is performed only after a thorough examination including medical, psychological, and psychiatric testing.
Hoar said there are two kinds, or forms, of exorcism, simple or minor forms and solemn or "major exorcism."
The United States Conference of Catholic Bishops describes exorcism as a prayer that falls in the category of "sacramentals."
"The Sacrament of Penance forgives our sins and reconciles us to the Church, renewing Baptism and bestowing grace to fight evil and grow in virtue," the conference website continues. "As a sacramental, exorcism prepares one for the grace of the Sacrament."
"Given the super abundance of confusing and inaccurate information available in the public arena surrounding this particular topic, the manner in which this revised rite is announced provides for a teachable moment to believers and non-believers alike," the conference states.
Hoar and Laffin plan to discuss the misconceptions surrounding exorcisms, the danger of "New Age" and "occult" practices which make people more vulnerable to demonic possession.
Praying the Rosary and the prayer of St. Michael the Archangel are powerful antidotes to the devil, Hoar said.
Hoar said he is planning to give a talk at Our Lady of the Assumption Chapel on Enders Island on Halloween, which will be followed by an extended 12-hour Eucharistic Adoration through 8 a.m. on Nov. 1, All Souls Day.
Thursday's event will begin at 7 p.m. with the interview, then a screening of the film followed by a brief audience Q&A.
